Values may contain inline HTML (e.g. bold) and HTML entities ( , &). To move another element under JSON control, give it data-ocx-content="some.path" and add a matching key here.

credits.eyebrow: Based on a study by Luke Gregor & Nicolas Gruber:
credits.title: Recent history of surface ocean acidification extremes that compound marine heatwaves   in   AGU Advances (2026)

intro.copy: Marine heatwaves and ocean‑acidification extremes increasingly strike the same waters at the same time — compound extremes that stress marine life far more than either event alone. Here is their recent history across the global ocean, 1982–2024.

definitions.title: How two extremes become compound
definitions.subtitle: A 2015 example · Hover each part to update the map

mhw.title: Marine Heatwave
mhw.desc: Sea-surface temperature in the top 5% of its historical record.

oax.title: Ocean Acidification Extreme
oax.desc: Hydrogen-ion concentration [H⁺] in the top 5% of its record.

cex.title: Compound Extreme
cex.desc: Both extremes in the same place and month.

method.title: How do we decide what is extreme?
method.intro: An extreme is unusual for that location and time of year—not simply the warmest or most acidic value on the map.
method.exampleHeading: One concrete example: estimating January's threshold

step1.title: Remove the long-term trend
step1.body: At every ocean pixel, we first remove a quadratic trend from the monthly SST and [H⁺] series. This keeps the focus on unusually strong departures while preserving changes in variability.

step2.title: Build the local record
step2.body: From each detrended 1° time series, we collect matching calendar months into local records: all Januaries together, all Februaries together, and so on.

step3.title: Respect the seasonal cycle
step3.body: January is compared with Januaries, July with Julys, and so on. A month is extreme when it exceeds its month-of-year 95th percentile. For our time series (43 years), this results in only two Junuaries, two Februaries, etc. being extreme in the same pixel.

step4.title: Find the overlap
step4.body: A compound extreme is recorded only when SST and [H⁺] both cross their local thresholds in the same pixel and month.

method.why: Why not a fixed baseline? With rapid warming and acidification, once-rare conditions quickly become common. Detrending lets us examine the processes that still create exceptional months within a changing ocean.

enso.title: El Niño – La Niña connection
enso.copy: Compound area peaks at the end of — or just after — El Niño events, often during the following La Niña. Hover a bar to trace that year in the table & map.

largest.title: The largest compound events
largest.copy: Hover a row to locate it on the map and highlight its year in the chart, or click a column heading to sort.

frequency.title: More common than chance
frequency.copy: The two hazards do not overlap randomly: circulation and stratification make their coincidence strongly latitude-dependent. Hover either figure to spotlight those latitudes on the map.

small.title: Most events are small
small.copy: Most common size ~500,000 km² — roughly the area of Spain — lasting a single month.

giants.title: But a few giants dominate
giants.copy1: The largest 20% of events contribute more than
giants.copy2: of the total compound-event area in the global ocean.

seasons.title: Summer is the danger season
seasons.copy: Compound extremes occur nearly twice as often in summer. Their latitude range expands poleward in summer and contracts toward the tropics in winter.

mechanism.title: The mechanism: a tug-of-war
mechanism.copy: During marine heatwaves, warming raises [H⁺], while changes in mixing and sDIC can oppose it. Drag the control to explore that balance, or choose The Blob for manuscript-derived event magnitudes.
